## Same seven notes, different boss

Play the white notes from D to D with a low D humming underneath. Every pitch
you touch belongs to C major, and yet C has lost its authority completely. The
drone appointed D, and once D is in charge every other note takes on a new job.
That B, a sixth degree that would sit lower in D minor, now reads as a distinct
brightness.

A *mode* is a step pattern heard around a chosen tonic. Rotate the major-scale
steps seven ways and you get Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian,
Aeolian and Locrian. Rotation settles the arithmetic in one line of Ruby. Your
ear needs more convincing than that, because seven notes with no anchor slide
straight back into the parent major scale you already know. The drone is what
stops the slide. It pins the address while the pattern moves around it.

## Seven rotations, one held D

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

define :build_scale do |root, steps|
  notes = [root]
  steps.each { |step| notes << notes[-1] + step }
  notes
end

define :play_mode do |root, steps|
  notes = build_scale(root, steps)
  in_thread do
    synth :dark_ambience, note: root - 12, sustain: 7.5,
      release: 0.5, amp: 0.45
  end
  (notes + notes[1..-2].reverse).each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.32
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

major_steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1]
names = [:ionian, :dorian, :phrygian, :lydian,
         :mixolydian, :aeolian, :locrian]

names.each_with_index do |name, index|
  puts name
  play_mode(note(:d4), major_steps.rotate(index))
  sleep 1
end
```

Every pass starts and ends on D, so root and pattern can't change together and
confuse the comparison. Lydian's raised fourth opens upward. Phrygian's lowered
second lies right against the tonic and crowds it. Mixolydian sounds like major
for most of its length, then declines to pull home, because the semitone under
the octave has gone. Keep the drone in your ear between passes; the
characteristic degrees are easiest to catch across a boundary.

Here's one to answer before you read further. Which of the seven felt least like
it had a home at all?

## Take things away and see what breaks

1. Cut the loop down to Ionian, Dorian and Mixolydian: major, minor with a
   raised sixth, and major with a lowered seventh. Find the one diagnostic note
   in each pass before you restore the other four modes.
2. Delete the drone thread. Nothing about the arrays changed and the centre gets
   much harder to hold. Notice which patterns collapse fastest into a nearby
   major scale once the low reference is gone.
3. Replace `:d4` with `:fs3` and keep the drone an octave below the new root.
   Every sounding pitch moves; the interval order and the modal identities do
   not.

## Rotation moves the semitones

Rotating an array preserves its seven values and changes their order. They still
sum to twelve, so every mode reaches its octave on schedule. What moves is where
the two semitones fall relative to the root, and moving them redistributes
tension across the whole scale.

Major and natural minor make handy reference points. Ionian is major. Dorian is
natural minor with a raised sixth, Phrygian is minor with a lowered second,
Lydian is major with a raised fourth, Mixolydian is major with a lowered
seventh, and Aeolian is natural minor exactly. Locrian lowers both the second
and the fifth, which leaves even its tonic triad without a perfect fifth to
stand on. Use those comparisons for listening; the step formulas remain the
definition.

A characteristic degree is evidence for a mode, never the whole of it. Write a
Dorian tune that never reaches degree 6 and you've written something your
listener will file under natural minor. This program climbs and descends through
every degree so no pattern can hide its identifying note. Real melodies do it
with duration, accent and repetition, which brings the note into focus without
turning the line into a scale exercise.

That shared D is the experimental control. Start each rotation on its own
white-key tonic and you'd change pitch height and tonal centre at the same time,
leaving the comparison uninterpretable. Applying all seven patterns to one root
forces interval order to carry the entire difference. There's a broader point
hiding in it too: Dorian doesn't belong to D and Mixolydian doesn't belong to G.
Any mode starts anywhere you like.

## Drill three modes against one drone

Build a ten-trial drill using Ionian, Dorian and Mixolydian, opening with
`use_random_seed 42`. Each trial picks a mode, sustains its drone, and plays a
six-note phrase that includes the characteristic degree. Leave four beats for
your answer before you print and replay the name.

Store the patterns as data and hold rhythm, register and synth fixed across all
ten. Do that and a correct identification has to come from the mode itself,
since you've removed every accidental cue the renderer could have offered.
